Question: What was the craziest behavior you saw as a server at a restaurant?
Answer: What was the craziest behavior you saw as a server at a restaurant? Most servers and bartenders see their fair share of idiotic and rude behavior, but one of the strangest/craziest moments I saw was on a random Tuesday night. It was a slow night with only a few patrons in the restaurant. I was behind the bar and was busy stocking and shutting down part of the bar for the evening. An older gentleman came in and sat at the bar and ordered a drink. He also had a guest with him, a full size cardboard cutout of John McCain. Suffice to say that I was both shocked and amused, but I managed to be professional and poured the drinks(he had ordered one for ‘John’) while not breaking into hysterical laughter. He later ditched the cutout outside by the benches. The other weird and crazy behavior was the couple who literally had their wedding in the Olive Garden I was working at. They had a dinner reservation, but failed to inform the manager that they were having the ceremony in the restaurant first. They and about 30+ people took over a section of the restaurant for over an hour without ordering anything. That was a weird and special night.

Question: What were the traits of the Greek god Ares?
Answer: What were the traits of the Greek god Ares? Ares was the sin of Zeus and Hera. Although he was the god of war he was written as violent, cowardly, and manipulative. The Greeks had little respect for him and most of the stories show that the other gods and goddesses detested him as well. The exception was Aphrodite, who was his lover. Ares was easily defeated by Hercules in battle and has very few positive traits in the myths. He was said to be from Thrace, a part of Greece which had warlike tribes. The Greeks were a practical people who saw the good and bad things in life. Ares represented the evils of war; wars fought for the wrong reasons. They had much greater respect for Athena, who was a strategic war goddess.

Question: Why are rhyming couplets common in Shakespearean sonnets?
Answer: Why are rhyming couplets common in Shakespearean sonnets? The sonnet, which got its start in Italy, eventually made its way to England. An Italian sonnet is traditionally composed of 14 lines with the first 8, or octave, outlining some problem and the closing 6 lines, or sestet, providing the solution. The English sonnet kept this 14 line structure, but changed the rhyme scheme and began using iambic pentameter, which gives 10 beats per line. This would become a very standard meter in many works of poetry and throughout much of William Shakespeare’s plays. The prevailing structure of the English sonnet has three quatrains (blocks of 4 lines) and a couplet. The usual set up of a sonnet was for the 3rd quatrain to provide the turn or volta, a sharp thematic twist. Shakespeare however liked to put his volta into the couplet, thus cementing his unique style. Sonnet 116 by William Shakespeare Let me not to the marriage of true minds (A) Admit impediments, love is not love (B) Which alters when it alteration finds, (A) Or bends with the remover to remove. (B) O no, it is an ever fixèd mark (C) That looks on tempests and is never shaken; (D) It is the star to every wand'ring bark, (C) Whose worth's unknown although his height be taken. (D) Love's not time's fool, though rosy lips and cheeks (E) Within his bending sickle's compass come, (F) Love alters not with his brief hours and weeks, (E) But bears it out even to the edge of doom: (F) If this be error and upon me proved, (G) I never writ, nor no man ever loved.
